blocks.x: This is a tape being recorded in the Howard Tilton Memorial Library Tulane University Seminar Room 2 and my name is Dick Allen what's yours? Marusi Mazzari. What's your full name?

Well it is... Alright, you don't want to give it... The real name you mean? Yeah. Well the real name is Rodolfo Mario Giuseppe Mazzari and with a name like that I was born on East 33rd Street. Yeah. So what's today's date? Today is the 6th I believe.
November the 6th, 1959. Yeah.
Alright. Well let's see Rudy.
When were you born?
I was born on March 25th, 1917.
March 25th, 1917. And where exactly you said?

Uh, 314 East 33rd Street in New York City. And how long you stood there? Oh I don't remember, I was too little. I know I got pushed around a lot because my father was always on the road with the opera company. So... I wound up on Bleeker Street. That I remember. I was about four or five years old but the cops were always coming looking for me and my brother. And that's how I remember Bleecker Street.
And that's how I remember Bleeker Street.
In the village, you know.
What were you doing? Playing bass underage or something?

No, I didn't even know bass existed in those days. I was living with my grandmother. My father couldn't take care of us because my mother died so he sent for his mother from Italy and set her up in an apartment house on Bleeker Street to take care of my brother Freddy, my sister Elsa and me. And my grandmother didn't know a word in English so I had a hard time learning English until I went to school, you know.
Well where did you go to school?
Public school number one, 102 I think it was, something like that. New York, they numbered schools instead of names, you know.
And how long did this go on that you went to school in New York and told you how old?

Until I was about seven, seven and a half, something like that. And then my father decided that he was doing pretty well financially, which he was. So he thought that he would give his children an education in Europe. And since he knew people in Italy, you know, having been born there, he just sent us over there. And, well my sister was the first one to leave. I think she came back to the States after two or three years. And my brother just about the same time. But actually I was the one who stayed the longest of all. I stayed ten years. And what did you study in Europe? Music. Mainly, but before that I studied a little architecture. And that didn't pan out so well for some reason or other. Can't you add? No, actually it had to do with geometry a lot, you know. But that wasn't the reason the reason I was because I was always getting in trouble with the other students. And finally I just got kicked out of the school. So you went into music, huh? Yeah. Or rather my father made me go into music. One day he brought home a bass fiddle and said, this is it for you. And that's been it for me ever since.
What did he play? Trumpet.
He was stage bandmaster with the Chicago Opera Company. He was stage bandmaster with the other people. He was stage bandmaster with the other people.

He was stage bandmaster with the other people. He was stage bandmaster with the other people. And did he ever play around the world on Turner Hay? Did you know? No. I think they might have come here on tour, you know. But he did remember New Orleans.
I suppose in the old days he came by with a, either the Chicago Opera or Metropolitan or something. I don't know whether they ever did hit this town in the old days. They probably did.
How did you have to come back to the States?

Well, I was going to school, studying in Venice. And I had about two more years to go and get a degree. And the war broke out. And I was an American citizen and all American citizens were urged to return to the States on account of the imminent pressing state of affairs. You know, Hitler was invading all over and it looked like there was going to be a war. So that's how I came back. And I've been here ever since. What did you come to when you first got back? Well, when I first came back, I wound up in Chicago. That's where the folks lived then, you know. And I stayed in Chicago about a year and I just played in Grand Park summer concerts. And I also got acquainted with playing in a dance band too. I didn't know a thing about playing in a dance band. Having come from school in Italy, you know. So I learned by playing Saturday night jobs here and there. First in Polish weddings or Italian weddings in Chicago. Little by little I learned how to play a beat, you know. You just don't play a dance beat just like that. You gotta learn it. So I picked that up and actually I hadn't been in Chicago, let's see, a few months. I got a job in Decatur, Illinois in a hotel, you know. And this thing lasted a whole summer. And this was a combination, dinner band and dance band. And I really learned a lot from that. Got so, I got a real swinging beat, you know. And I got so good at it, the band, in fact the whole band got so good, they were asked to stay. But I had already written a contract to go to Indianapolis with the Indianapolis Symphony. So I had to leave and that was, by the way, my first year with the Indianapolis Symphony. Which was the last about nine years engagement. And then what did you do after you left Indianapolis? Well, actually, this last year I hadn't signed up for the coming year. Yeah, I hadn't signed up a contract. And I was in New York and I was in the union there, a musician's union. And I met this Italian man and he said, oh, you play bass? He says, you're Italian. He was impressed by the fact that I spoke Italian. He says, I got a good job for you. He says, I, we got a fine orchestra in New Orleans, a symphony. He says, an Italian conductor, his name is Massimo Freccia. He says, you, you come down there, you'll be happy. It's warm all the time. He says, well, actually, I was, I really wanted to make a change anyway. So it didn't take very much to persuade me. I mean, I, I signed up right there and then, and that's how it happened. It comes to New Orleans. And that was, I came, the first year that Massimo Freccia started conducting the New Orleans Symphony.
And, uh, what year was that?
Oy yoy yoy.
Well, you had how many years in Indianapolis?
Nine.
And you came here back to this country what year? Yeah.
Uh, thirty-nine, no, thirty-eight. Thirty-eight. Something like that.
How long were you, was it before you got with the Indianapolis Symphony?
Well, I was with them nine years.
Yeah, but when you came back to this country, you didn't get with them immediately, huh?
Well, actually, within the year. Within the year.
Oh, yeah. So, let's see. Was, uh, then it was, uh, forty-eight when you came down here, huh?

Yeah. Just about that time. About forty-eight. I'd have to look it up in the files because, boy, I'm very bad with dates. Mm-hmm. I don't mean dates with girls, but I mean, as far as nineteen this, nineteen that, and June, and January. Yeah. Did you hear any jazz when you came down here? Oh, yeah. I certainly did. Uh, in fact, uh, that's one of the reasons why I was lured down here, because I had heard of the famous New Orleans jazz. Mm-hmm. And, of course, being a musician, you'd, you'd always want to hear something different, something new. And I was very impressed by it, and I also got to play it, you know, and it was quite difficult for me for a while to do it, but then I, I began to feel that two beat, you know. Yeah. And, uh, before you knew it, I, I was playing every Saturday nights, Friday nights, Sunday nights, and before you know it, I was playing Dixieland. Who were you playing with? Oh, I was playing with a lot of pick-up-the-last-minute bands, you know, out of the Union. And, uh, most of them, that's what they were. And, of course, there was, there was always interesting musicians in it. And so happened that, uh, I was playing Jobs, and there was, they were in Fazola playing clarinet, you know. And, uh, all things like that kind of scared me, because I knew he was a famous guy, and here I was, practically a greenhorn. At least I considered myself that. And I also got to play, uh, all the shows that came in at the Civic. Broadway shows, musical productions, you know. So, before you knew it, there I was.
How was it working with the Zell now?

Oh, it was fine. Uh, actually, I met him, first time was when I, we were doing one of the Broadway shows. I came down at the Civic. And, uh, I remember it was during an intermission and a rehearsal. Uh, he very casually turned around to me and says, come on, let's go have a beer. So, I just followed him. There was a little joint in the alley there that sold beer and oysters and everything. And, uh, I'm sitting there drinking a beer, and sure enough, it was Faz already on his second, he'd already gone on his second beer. And he'd ordered some oysters. And he told the guy, just keep opening, man, just keep opening. And I think he ate three dozen oysters just like that. It was, so, you know, that kind of threw me for a while. I didn't, wow. But then, after I got to know Faz better, you know, I realized, well, that's the way he was. He just ate and drank beer, man, or something like it. I don't know whether, maybe that had anything to do with playing the Albert system, you know, in the clarinet, but maybe it was a little harder, extra harder to play, so he consumed all that stuff. Maybe it makes you thirsty, you have to produce more wind. Yeah, could be. No, I think it's all in the, in the fingering. No, it has a bigger bore, too.
Yeah, it does. So, and they have, usually have a wider lay in the reed, you know, so that the more wind, maybe that makes you thirsty. Maybe that's why, you know, why so many of them end up lushes.
Yeah.
Well, playing really does make you thirsty. I've noticed that.

Oh, yeah, well, it does. I always, it got so, I always had a drink of beer whenever I was on a job. I mean, I just had to have it, you know, especially when you wrap yourself around a bass fiddle, something out beats.
How long did you know Fazz before he died?
Oh, let's see. I think I only know him about a year. I had just met him and just began a good friendship with him, you know.
Were you with him pretty steady?

Well, I always wound up playing jobs, you know, in the same band and several times, well, you know, Fazz, he was, he was so popular that people would just beg him, I said, please come down to my joint and play even if it's only, all right.

a couple of tunes or something, you know. And he would. I mean, he'd try to go to all these places, but if he tried to go to all of them, there wouldn't be enough time in the day. So he tried to make the few ones that he could, and he asked me if I would care to go along with him, you know. And I said, sure. So I learned a lot by going after him, and I learned how popular he was and how well he played, and I got to know a lot of things about him that I didn't know. And he really was. I mean, you could tell when he walked into a place, even if it was to play a set, maybe, you know. Boy, the joint would really start getting a feel, you know. He was a very remarkable guy.
How did the other musicians react when he came here?

Oh, they'd just break out in a big smile, you know. If they had been bored, well, they weren't bored anymore when he walked in, I'll tell you that. The guy actually would throw sunshine. That's how good he was. Not only his plane, but his personality. He was a nice guy. He really was. He was a good Joe. Just ate too much, huh? Yeah, too many oysters. I guess.
I think that's what killed him. I'm not sure. All that easy.

Well, I suppose, ooh, too much beer, too. I suppose. I don't know. But I was surprised when I went to the funeral. He had got flowers from famous bandsmen, you know, throughout the country. And, I mean, the big-name bands all sent flowers. And he had people at his funeral. It was fantastic. Well, anyway, that's how I got to meet people from New Orleans, you know. And I really enjoyed it. I really got the feel of what New Orleans is, you know. What New Orleans jazz is.
Well, what else would you describe that goes into that? The feel of New Orleans and jazz and all that.

Oh, gee, I don't know whether I understand what you're trying to ask me. I mean, what goes for the... I mean, what makes you New Orleans New Orleans? Well, I guess the people, too, are very different. I mean, for instance, you hear Otto Thomas always saying about the mixed Brooklyn that Orleanians have in their accent, you know. That impresses people, too, you know. And, well, it's just like, like, you see a guy down the street and say, where you at, Joe? You know, where you at? That...
Mm-hmm.

And a lot of things like that that you can't put your finger on, but there are there, you know. And, of course, the food. You know, I'm Italian. I've been brought up with good food. I was very, very glad when I got in New Orleans because the first thing I found out was, boy, there was good food. And I was getting so tired of that Middle West. Same old stuff every day. That, I don't know, they just don't know how to cook, you know. They have no imagination. So that's another reason why I was glad to be in New Orleans. Yeah. In fact, my first meal that I had was in Arnault, I think, went in there. And they had one of those... It was lunchtime and it was very cheap. I think a dollar or something like that. Boy, I got tremendous lunch for that. I got introduced to New Orleans that way.
Now, you know Sharky, huh?

Well, yeah, I knew him while I was working at WDSU. I was a record librarian. Of course, Sharky always came in and played tapes for recordings, you know, for Capitol, wasn't it? Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm. So I got to hear him through that and I learned a lot about jazz, which I didn't know, you know. And, of course, being a librarian in a record library radio station is quite an experience. And I think that's how I got to learn a lot of things. And, oh, by the way, you know, one day Frank Assunto was due to make a tape for overseas servicemen, you know, and all the guys showed up except the bass player. So they called his home. They called his parents and they couldn't find them anywhere. Well, they finally thought, well, he must be in some movie in town because he couldn't find them anywhere else. And he liked to watch Western movies. Well, they didn't have time to go and search every movie house in New Orleans. So Pete Lotteman, who happened to be musical director of WDSU, says, well, why don't you use Rudy? He's a bass player. He's right here. So Frank says, crazy, man. So I sat in and I played a tape with Frank Assunto, man. That was a real joy, believe me. I was very happy to do it. Of course, it was a benefit and all that. It really made me feel great, you know.
Was anybody in Chaggy's band outstanding?
Well, they all were outstanding. I mean, to me, the whole thing was just one outstanding body.
Oh, yeah.
Let's put it that way. He was doing a lot of engagements in the Pond House in Chicago. Does he still go there now? Or does he bother to go out? I don't know.
He traveled some. I don't know if he's been up there like that.
He still does. Well, anyway, I was always looking forward when he came to WDSU because he was making the recording sessions and sessions, you know. I really enjoyed that. It was a kick.
Have you ever seen any colored bands around?

Mm-hmm. Not until recently, though, I'd heard about the colored bands, but somehow or other, I never seemed to have, you know, dug one until one day. And then, uh, Pete Loderman mentioned the fact that Papa Celestin was coming to the station to do a session. And so, naturally, I got all shook up because I was being my first colored band, you know. And sure enough, when comes this venerable old man, man, I'll never forget. And here comes these other cats, and they sit down there, and they start going, and that was a real wonderful experience. Oh, Papa, he's done going, huh?
Mm-hmm.
I also, uh, well, let's see, only this year was I able to dig my first funeral. I don't mean my funeral, but I mean a colored funeral.
Yeah. Like, uh... Did you dig the graves?

No, I didn't dig them. I dig them. I dug the music, man. Mm-hmm. That was real crazy. I, uh, had been listening to you talk about colored funerals, and I'd heard about other people talk about colored funerals. And, of course, uh, I wanted to make one sooner or later. Mm-hmm. And one fine day, uh, let's see, where did we go? We went to, uh, Algiers. Way across... No, this one was over in, uh, uptown somewhere.
Gee, I'm trying to remember. Maybe at 8th and Daniel Street. That was, that's where I was.

The Elks Hall there. It used to be the Bulls. That was my first one, and I was surprised when I got there. There were artists with their sketching pads and pencils and pens and all kinds of people with cameras. And, uh, I just enjoyed it from beginning to the end. It was tremendous. And those dirages they play are indescribable. And, uh, although I've seen it written in magazines about those funerals, I, I still don't think it, they can be described. One has to see them from beginning to end to realize what they are. I mean, what a great big kid they are. The color is so much... It's... Undescribable. I, I went to a second one. I think the second one I went was in Algiers. Walked all day in the sun, hot, scorching sun. But I stuck with it. Right. And of course you were there, you were always at all of them.
Sun never seems to worry me too much, you know. Somehow the music's going.
That's a funny thing.
When the music stops, you're exhausted.

Boy, I'll say. Then you notice all of a sudden. When it's all over, you realize. And you come to, and you realize how tired you are. And then there's that long trek home too. But you got something that stays with you for the next two or three days. And I find myself, after that, I find myself trying to persuade my friends to see one. I really do. And I said, you'll be sure to go see one. Because they're just wonderful. And they really are. In fact, when I go to Italy, I'm going to try and describe the Italian people. Those colored funerals. Because they're really. That's authentic New Orleans. If there ever was.
Well, who all did you meet as you walk along with them?

Well, you meet all kinds of people. Surprisingly enough, people which you've never seen before. All of a sudden, here you are talking to somebody you've never known before. And as you follow the parade. And sometimes it's just a lady who lives in the neighborhood. And she's lugging her child along with her, you know. Like little Sammy. I remember that time in Algiers. We lugged him. We took turns in carrying him. And of course, you meet the musicians too. And that's a great big thing. They always greet you and make you feel like you're the greatest person in the world. And actually, you're only coming there to listen and follow, you know. It's a real great thing.
They really treat you with respect, you know.
Mm-hmm. And they talk to you and want to know all about you. It's amazing.
You ever hear many good tuba players down here?
Well, oh, yes, I have. You're talking about swinging tubas or?
Well, swinging tubas. I was particularly interested in.
Well, no, but I understand that Mr. Finanza used to play a Dixieland tuba. Well, that was before he joined the New Orleans Symphony, though, wasn't it?
Yes, we've got records of them here from about 24.

Oh, well, you know that I never did hear him play a swing tune on the tuba. Because I met him when I started with the symphony, and of course that's, you know, straight lace. But I had no idea that he played a swing tuba. I understand he played quite a swing tuba. He was very, very famous at it.
Well, did you hear many tuba players with a dance band here?
No, I haven't. But the brass bands now. The brass, of course. Yeah.
You've heard them. Well, let's see, I made some questions up. I might as well ask about those. What about that lady you met in Mississippi, Southern Bell?

Oh. Oh, yes. You mean the time I came? Well, I took a trip to New York, and on the way down back to New Orleans, I stopped at some friends in Mississippi. Yeah, yeah. Well, that shook me up pretty bad. If I remember correctly, I was invited.

for supper at a real southern Mississippi family's house and of course his friend had been invited along too, you know, and well they were very hospitable, you know, and all that and we were having dinner and everything was going along fine until, oh, I think we were carrying a conversation about Italy and this lady of course kept shooting questions at me about Italy, she wanted to know what the people did and how they did it and all that and then came the bomb and she says, well, we Christians don't do things that way. That really shook me up man. I really didn't know what to say.

Yeah, I don't know what to say because the tape's about to run off, why don't we let it run off? Just let it rip. Okay. The first thing I want to know is, see as you're calling up leave, is what did George Washington say when he crossed the Delaware?
Oh, he said, fa no cazzo di freddo. Good. That's out of the way.
I thought I told you how to say that, didn't I? You did, but I wanted to get it down on tape so I could practice. Okay. Now let's see, Savitsky was in Indianapolis, huh?
Yes, he was. Old Fabian, we used to call him Beanie because he came from Boston. Dick? Mm-hmm. That's all I'm being.
And what was he like?
Oh, he was a...
Yeah, that's a he.
Well, we don't want to put this tape on the censored file and nobody will hear it that way so...
Yeah, we can put it in a censored file.
Let's just suggest.
Whatever you want to do.

Well, I didn't care much for him for the fact that he didn't care much for me. He made it pretty miserable on me when I... All the nine years I worked over there for some reason or other. Of course, he was a strict old country Russian type, you know. And I don't know, it seems to me he had a grudge against something and he was taking it out on people. He made it tough for a lot of good musicians over there. He's teaching at the University of Miami now. Married into big money, you know. As a conductor, he never did make it very much. How's that level doing? Yeah, it's pretty good. Well, anyway, he was a bass player originally. And, I don't know, somehow or other somebody put it in his head that he was a conductor. So he became a conductor. He was married to this Maria Kusevitsky, related to the Serg Kusevitsky, the famous Boston Symphony Orchestra conductor. And, you know, one thing pulled and money and the other. But, before you know it, the guy's got a baton in his hands and he's conducting the Indianapolis Symphony. And, I was at the Musicians' Union in Chicago one day, shooting the bull with all the musicians, you know. Like in New York, in Chicago, all the big towns. When you're not working, all you do is go to the union and stay there all day long. And, there was a letter on the bulletin board that says, young musicians, if you want to audition, there are openings for so many violins, so many violins, so many violins, so many cellos, and so many basses in the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra. And, auditions will be held for so many of the day. So I picked up my bass today and went up there and I was at one of the swanky hotels in Chicago with a Blackhawk I think it was. Blackstone, Blackstone. And there were quite a few young guys from Chicago and good musicians auditioning. And we noticed that as they came out of the audition, they were all shook up. They were either pale white in the face or shaking or something. So I was thinking, gee, this guy must be real tough, you know. So I went in there and I did my audition. And he asked me, he says, what is your name? And I told him, he says, how old you are? I said, well, I'm 19 years old. You are sure? And he says, well, play something. So I played a little something and then he gave me something to sight read. And he says, all right, that's enough. Sit down. So I sat down and he says, how you would like to play in my orchestra? Just like that. I said, well, I like it fine. He says, all right. He says, it paid $35 a week. 20-week season. But you must practice. If you don't practice, it's too bad, you know. So that was it. And out I go, you know, I kept practicing, all right. And the season opened, came up and I packed my bags and went to Indianapolis. And boy, oh boy, when rehearsals started, it was tough. This guy was, he would make you play one by one, you know, stop the orchestra. Instead of rehearsing what was important, he'd just make everybody play one by one. He's wasting time. So he's making everybody nervous. And before he knew it, we got his number. And naturally, being a bass player, he made it tough on bass players. And, you know, this got to be a drag after a while. Play one by one alone all the time. Gee, he started getting nervous. He got the idea also that he would teach the bass section and give them a lesson every week. So every once a week, we had to go to Jordan Conservatory and line up and have him give us a lesson. Well, I got so, every time it was my turn, he would say, Mazzari, you are flat. Go home and practice. And the next week, it'd be, Mazzari, you are sharp. Go home and practice. And he wouldn't let me play two notes, you know, something like that. So, one fine day, I don't know what hit me, but it was my turn to play. So I said, well, how do you want it today, Dr. Flat or Sharp? And I got a pink slip right there because all the other bass players laughed. By the way, there are testimonies that I originated that joke in case anybody wants to steal it. I'm the originator of it because I have seven other witnesses. I'm familiar with Fabian, but I doubt if he won't testify to it, you know. So I got the pink slip that time. I got a letter from the manager. It says, it is my painful duty to inform you that your services are no longer required. So I went through the whole summer wondering when I was going to get a job next winter, of course. I never worked in the summer, hardly. You know, it's pretty hard for a musician to get jobs in the summer. Meanwhile, the union in Indianapolis met and decided that since I was a local member of the union, that I should have a job. And so when Fabian started to import a bass player from New York, from out of town, they said, uh-uh, Mazzari here is a local guy and I think we should use him. Well, that made Fabian very mad, so he made him play another audition. So I remember by that time he got into this kick about auditioning guys in a dark theater where you couldn't see where he was and you were on the stage all alone with all the lights they could dig up, you know, on you. Isn't that ridiculous?
Yeah.

So I played and then while I was playing, he said, that's enough! So I walked off and about a few minutes later, the manager of the orchestra, Mr. Frank Minor was his name, he came over and he says, well, he says, uh, uh, Dr. Svisky has decided to let you join the orchestra again, but you must try to practice, you must try to improve. He says, he thinks you're doing very badly. And funny part of ours is that everybody else said that I was doing a real singing job, playing bass, you know. So I went through, oh, years and years of that. Same old thing. Like he used to do with the other guys, stop the orchestra and play one by one, which is a very bad thing to do. It makes you nervous in the first place. And don't ask me why, but it is, it does make you. And finally, uh, I, I just got to thinking, well, I gotta make a move here, you know, this is no good. So that's how I happened to hold out one, one summer. I didn't sign a contract. And sure enough, this New Orleans deal came in and here I am. I'm glad that I held out.
Did Hill, uh, let's see, did Heifetz ever play with you when you were there? Oh, in, in Indianapolis? Uh-huh.

Oh, yes. And how? Heifetz played many times. I remember, he used to come every year. In fact, I remember one year, we're scheduled to do a Beethoven violin concerto. And, uh, of course, uh, Szyzki always had to rehearse the orchestra part first. Very important, you know. I remember one time, he was, every time he came to the bass passages, which are very prominent in Beethoven, he would just say, bass is too loud, bass is too loud. So he got us cut down to a whisper. Well, uh, the day when Heifetz came to rehearse with the orchestra, uh, played about a few bars and he stops the orchestra and talks to Szyzki, you know. Szyzki's already been back with him. And Heifetz is looking toward the basses, you know. So, again, we play, and again, we stop. And Heifetz, this time, raises his voice loud enough for us to hear. He says, I want more basses. So, Szyzki's arguing with him, you know. So, he turns to the basses and he says, a little more basses, you know. And Heifetz, by this time, is looking at the basses and he's giving the sign, which he doesn't ordinarily do. He's very, he always told the conductor, you know, what to do. Fine fellow, by the way. And, uh, again, we play, and again, Heifetz stops the orchestra. And finally, uh, Fabian says, well, all right. He says, we play it the way you want to. After all, it is your concerto. And Heifetz says, yes, and Beethoven wrote it, you know.
That's a great idea. All right.
It's guys like that that always get it sooner than later, huh? Mm-hmm.
And what about, uh, Stokowski? Did you have a little bit of him? Oh, yeah.
I played on Stokie.
Something for my code.

Oh, it sounds good. I wonder if that's coming through the tape. I hope so. Yeah. Oh, you go ahead. Some more. After you. Okay. Yes, I did play with Leopold. And, uh, well, that was a long time ago. I'm noble. It took me a long time before I did get to play with Leopold, because, as a matter of fact, I never did play with him until he came to New Orleans here, and he made the famous walkout scene, you know? He came during Mardi Gras season, and you know how the auditorium is divided in two parts. Well, the small part was booked for the symphony concert, and the other part was booked for the Mardi Gras ball, you know? And we were doing Manuel de Falla something. El Amor Brudo, I think it was. And we kept hearing these noises of this band on the other side, you know? Chum, pa-chum, pa-chum, pa-chum. And, uh, well, uh, old Stokey didn't dig that, so he made a famous walk-off-the-stage scene, which made headlines. I enjoyed playing with him. I think he's a real slinging conductor. He... He phrases, you know? He doesn't stand there and beat time, like a high school orchestra or something. Guy early phrases things and you feel...
the beat just the same. What kind of a guy was Massimo Freccia?

Well, Massimo Freccia was a very nice person, personally. I mean, he was. He's conducting in Italy now, you know. In fact, I came in the same year he came in. And, uh, I was a record librarian. That's how I got to know Massimo Freccia a little better than the average musician in the orchestra through music. Of course, he had a hard time with this, uh, just trying to explain to the musician what he wanted. I mean, you know, he would stop the orchestra and you could see it in his eyes, you know, that he could see all the score in front of him and he was trying to tell him what he wanted, but his English just didn't come up to it. And many times he'd just stop the orchestra and try to explain it and nothing would come out. So he'd just say, well, just play, play. So that was Massimo Freccia.
And Alexander Hillsberg. What did you do?

Oh, Alexander Hillsberg. He's conducting the orchestra right now, huh? Well, I played on the Hillsberg full season and then I was only called in as extra strings were needed. But fortunately, uh, I, Hillsberg was one of the conductors who didn't pick on me and we got along real fine together. He, of course, he used to be the concert maister with the Philadelphia orchestra, you know. Fine violinist. And, uh, he has that nice smile, you know, how are you? You know, grin. Have you been practicing this summer? You know, things like that.
Well, give me the full treatment on that, man. Don't go back.
Well, let's see, uh, I can't really think of much. Or rather I'm not in a vain to describe him.
His accent is pretty hard. But they say the, uh, musician comes back. He said one year out of the conservatory and he's coming back in the fall, the one season with the Hillsberg.

Oh, yes. And he would greet the orchestra and he would say, I am very happy to have you again in my orchestra. I've been practicing this summer. We are going to find out if you have been practicing. And, uh, sure enough, if you haven't been, I mean, he raises hell, you know. He can tell? Well, I don't know whether they can tell or whether they just pick on somebody, but they have a knack for, I think, a lot of them stop because they're lost and they have to find an excuse for having stopped the orchestra, you know. And so they just pick out anything. And the first guy they lay their eyes on and that's it. We got a lot of conductors which aren't what they should be. I mean, after, I haven't played in an orchestra for so long, you can tell, especially if you know your part, you've been playing, say you've been playing Beethoven's Fifth for so many years and you just, I got so, I hardly looked at the music. I would just look at the conductor, you know, because I practically knew what was coming next. So you, you get to tell if a conductor really knows what he wants or what he's undecided or what he doesn't know what he's doing or what he's... And I tell you, a lot of them just don't.
Who's the best that you've worked under?

Well, I think the best conductor I worked under was Arthur Wierczynski. I mean, he was a real fine, fine musician. And where was this? Well, this was in New Orleans. He was guest conductor. And also, I think I played under him in Indianapolis, if I remember correctly. Well, to me, as far as the conductors that I've played under, of course, to my estimation, the best conductor there is, is Ernest Ansarmette, the conductor of the Orchester de la Suisse Romande. I mean, from the recordings I've heard, I like his interpretations. That reminds me of a joke. I mean, the guy really knows what he's doing. He just can bring out color, out of a score. Like, he's terrific. He's very good. And as far as the opera conductors, I think Alberto Heredia is a very fine opera. He's a real swinging opera conductor.
Did you work with any great guest soloist?

Oh, yes. Of course. Oh, I can't remember all of them. A lot of violinists, cellists, sopranos, you know, like, ooh, Sigeti, Heifetz, Francescati. Well, naturally, anyone who does play in a symphony orchestra gets to see all those people, you know.
What would they like? How did they impress you?

Oh, uh, now, I, one person I liked as a soloist, a famous musician, was Nathan Milstein. I liked him. He was a real nice boy. He, uh, would always talk to everybody. And, in fact, you know, would always show up rehearsals before he was time to come on stage. And he's always, invariably, sit in the second fiddle sessions and read the second fiddle part. In fact, one time in Indianapolis, he was sitting in the second fiddle doing that and he came in wrong all by himself and said, let's go, stop the orchestra. He says, who did that? And Milstein raised his bow and everybody laughed. He plays fine, very fine violinist too.
Well, you asked me to ask you about Walter Herbert, who is he?

Walter Herbert? Oh, he conducted the opera orchestra here in New Orleans for many years. In fact, he was practically the business manager too. And when they hardly had any money, you know, I think he managed it very well. And if we have an opera orchestra in New Orleans, an opera company in New Orleans today, I think he's to thank for it. Because of his iron fist was money. And he was, and a fine orchestra conductor too. Throw cue at musicians, throw cues at singers, everything. He was very good. I liked him as an opera conductor.
Who's this fellow, Fontana, you asked me?

Oh, Fontana is an old Italian immigrant from Milan, Italy, who came here and came here with an opera. I think they got stranded here. So he'd been here ever since. He was a trombone player and he wound up as a orchestra manager at Sanger, the old Sanger Theatre, you know? And then he became a personnel manager with the symphony here. Ettore Fontana. He was a real nice fellow. He was, in fact, he booked all the Broadway musicals at the Civic and that's how I got to play them all, you know? Because he hired me every time.
And that made him especially nice, I guess.

Oh, yes. That was good money, you know? On the pit, you know, play nine, ten shows, you get a hundred and fifty, a hundred and sixty, a hundred and seventy dollars. I used to do the ice shows too when they came to town here. Same thing, good money. But since he died, somebody else took charge of all these big job deals and all of a sudden I was out. It's politics, you see? You're in one day, out the other.
What was Fontana's personality like?

Oh, he was a very unassuming person. He didn't try to put on an act like some people do. He was very pleasant and affable. And he tried to, of course, being a personnel manager is quite a job, you know? You got to please the conductor and you got to please the musicians too. You're the guy in the middle. Boy, that's a hell of a job to be in. Of course, the first thing you know is if something happens, oh, they'll say he's kissing the conductor's ass, you know? Things like that. But I think Fontana did a pretty good job of it. And having known several personnel managers in various orchestras, I think Mr. Fontana was by far the best. He was nice to talk to. We always talked in Italian together. Of course, being from Milan, he talked, he knew his Milanese dialect, but he talked pure Italian too when he wanted to. So I enjoyed talking to him.
What's pure Italian?

Pure Italian is like, it's spoken as it is written in books. You know, Italy has a lot of dialects. For instance, there is a Venetian dialect where I'm from. Well, if I spoke Venetian dialect to a Sicilian, he wouldn't understand me. And if a Sicilian spoke a Sicilian dialect to me, I wouldn't understand him. But if we spoke the mother language, straight Italian, we would understand each other. I think there's something like that in Germany too, isn't it? Parts of Germany.
Well, they have different dialects. I like to have high and low German. Yeah.
All that. But that doesn't pertain to English for some reason or other, except the accents. Yeah.
You and I can understand each other pretty well.
Yeah, we've gotten along real fine.
Well, who is Paul Kosserbaum?

Oh, Paul Kosserbaum is an old time drummer, old New Orleanian from way back. He's a real nice boy. He... I didn't meet him until I came down to New Orleans and played in the symphony here. He was playing with Bill Hall. Bill Hall was in charge of the percussion section. And of course, invariably, there are two men back there, you know, to play the bass drum, the snare drums, the triangles, the bells, you know, how the percussion section is in the symphony orchestra. And I got to meet Paul Kosserbaum and he's a very quiet, easy going fellow. And he'd been living... He was born here in New Orleans and lived here all his life. And a very nice cat.
You don't remember any little anecdotes about him or Fontana or anybody else?
Oh, no, not off the handle, I couldn't tell you. I mean...
What about Xavier University? What is that?

Oh, uh, yes, Xavier University. Well, I tell you. Uh... Oh, just about the last year before I left New Orleans, Cliff Richter played viola in the symphony and I was playing bass, of course. And, uh, Cliff was teaching at Xavier and he was a very ardent lover of Bach and chamber music and so on and so forth. And through his efforts, he finally taught a mother, what's her name there, who was in charge of the school, to put on some chamber music, Xavier. And he would guarantee that there, you know, there would be a success. And so finally, I guess, after talking a long time, he began a series of these things. And sure enough, there was a packed house every time. We put these things on on a Sunday afternoon. And they were very enjoyable. And they were, I mean, uh, any musician... And there were stuff with

who plays classical music, dreams of the time when you can play a little chamber music, because actually you're playing one part and you're playing it all along and you're the only guy doing it, and boy, it's just a real kick to hear yourself playing a certain line. Well anyway, these concerts were very, very successful. In fact, so successful that Alexander Hillsburg attended them, at least one of them, you know, and that was quite a thing to drag him out of there. He usually doesn't go and listens to very many things, but these were very, very good. And you know, chamber music, the old days actually has something to do with the jazz of today. You know, there are so many men in a group, and each man has something to play differently. It's the same thing like a jazz band, you know. It's chamber music, that's what it is. Sure.
How many men did you have out there?
Well, it varied. It'd be about 14 men on the stage.
And who were some of them?

Well, mostly we were all symphony fellas. And of course there would be a lot of fellas that came in and only played one number and that was it, you know. And we got paid for two. It was very remarkable that a thing like that would start Xavier University, you know. Somebody had to start it, had to be somewhere, and that was it. It goes to show you what a swinging university that is. Did you ever work with the summer pops? Oh yes. Sure, I worked many years with the summer pops. Yeah. We used to be out there and rehearse in the morning and the scorching sunlight out in the, what is it, what's the name of that square? Congo Square. Congo Square. Congo Square, yeah. They don't call it Congo Square now, do they?
Call it Boriga. But some people call it Congo Square. Boriga. They still call it Congo Square? Some of them do.

They still call it. They still call it the night. I, well anyway, the stage was set up over there and we'd rehearse every morning over there and then play the concerts at night. I enjoyed playing the pops very much. I think New Orleans enjoyed having it too. You can tell by the attendance. And, uh. My dear boy, what are you doing?
I think I am of a module idea.
You had too much blood for supper tonight.

Thank you. Do you know that that's what they used to call Poet Wine? One night I was down at the Apex Apartments and, uh, that the band had a rehearsal where they rehearsed numbers like The Saints and this was Emil Bond's band and they rehearsed, uh, Our Society. And I'll never forget Emil Bond's saying, hey man, give me some more of that blood, you know, and then eat down that wine and drink that wine. Oh yeah? And that's the first time I ever felt a whole building really shot, rock, you know. It was really, it was rocking. You heard, you know, rocking and rhythm and the joint is jumping and the place is really rocking tonight. But it was, a whole floor board and everybody was there. Aye, aye. Ralston Crawford, you know Ralston? Yeah. He and I were the only outside of that. Everybody else was musicians or neighborhood people. It was really
something. Blood? That was port wine? I wonder if they call all red wine. They call all red wine?

I think all red wine probably. But I think it was port that night. And you know, a brother, the guy with one eye who plays a harmonica and drives a junk wagon around the French Quarter, we were recording him one day and he was talking about that old wine. And I told him, yeah, I want to drink wine sometimes myself. And so he says, yeah, I like that. They got all kinds of wine. They got the toque and they got the burgundy wine. At least he didn't say burgundy wine. Oh, good for him. Yeah. He says, and they got salt-trygling. He says, and then they got white-poked and they got black-poked. Well, don't mind if I do. Let's see, what were we talking about anyhow? I was going to ask you something. We were talking about blood.
Oh, no. No. Oh, blood. The Italians say that wine makes blood, you know. Well, so does the French.
Yeah. Yeah. It makes your blood strong and healthy. That's what it would be. Let's face it. It does warm you up. Yeah, it does. It's a cold night at that.
It is a cold night at that. No. And, uh... Oh, right here. Okay. You want some blood?

Well, no, not blood. Blood from whales? It's got... I don't know. It's a squawk one. So, uh, I want to talk to you about playing the string bass. Oh, yeah, man. Okay. Ask me. How do you play the string bass pizzicato properly as compared with the way the jazz musicians play?
Well, uh, any good, uh, symphony bass player will play pizzicato properly and it's very easy to see why the, why the bass player is holding, is doing it. I mean, uh...
How does he hold his hand, for example? What about the fingerboard? Does he do anything with that?

Well, uh, you're getting... Okay. Too many questions at once. Too many questions at once. Okay. I'll tell you, uh... Don't get excited. Of course, uh... Am I interrupting you? More and more, you see now, good bass players playing jazz. Mm-hmm. Uh, you can, you can tell right away, you walk into a place and there's a band and you see a bass player. He's got his fingers on his strings, nice and straight, you know, and his elbow sticks out.
Mm-hmm.
And level with his arm, you know, and you can tell that he's had a good schooling and, and...
Well, now where should the thumb be placed?
Well, right behind, between the second and third finger.
Behind the neck and between the second and third fingers. Yeah. It's all in the middle there.

Yeah, and a lot of guys, they just let the thumb stick up, you know, and they, and they just move their fingers up and down. Well, that's a hard way to do it. I mean, they're just making it harder on themselves. But of course, those are the guys who didn't study. They just picked up a bass and they call themselves bass players. Mm-hmm. Of course, they, they may know, some of them know the chords, but most of them don't. Actually, if, if it's, the guy is a good enough, intelligent enough fella who has the, you know, the... Well, that he goes out and tries to make things easier for him, he's better off. Mm-hmm. But you can tell the difference right away, a bass player. We're just looking at him, you can tell whether he's... been raised to play the bass correctly or whether he just picked it up. Of course, more good bass players now are getting into the jazz group now, you know. I can tell you a very successful one in town is Bob Ciccarelli.
Yeah, I was thinking about him.

Oh man, he does a terrific job. Well, there you are, you see, he had the advantage of having started playing symphony bass. He studied it properly. Now he can walk into any band and play anything or... because he plays everything in position. Can play all those runs and to him, they come easy. Uh, a lot of those cats I was telling you about, you just, you just can't do it.
They're out of tune then, if they don't play them in position, is that what that... Out of tune, they jump all over the board, up and down, you know.
That's, that's...
How many strings do they play on those guys who don't know much?
Boy, I don't know. There's four strings. I doubt if they use them all. In other words, you see some real bad bass players sometimes. It just makes you...
When you were a kid, did you see many three-string basses in Italy?

Oh yeah, yeah. In fact, that's all there was. My teacher had a three-string bass in Italy, and that's all there was. In the, in the years of the famous bass player Giovanni Bottezzini, they just had G, D and A, and A was the lowest string in the bass. And it was only recently, I'd say about, ooh, the last 50 years that the E string was added to a bass fiddle.
Wait a second, Rudy. You're talking about three-string basses, famous bass players in Italy.

And how the change has come over to fourth string, huh? Yes. In fact, some fellow in Germany, or even further than that, he invented a machine for the E string, which is the lowest string, and it brings it chromatically down to a C by pushing levers. And a lot of symphony bass players use that. It goes way down to a low C, which is very deep, boom, see, chromatically, you know. Stepwise. E natural, E flat, and way down the line. Half a step at a time, I mean.
Yeah. And what's, what that means.

And of course, that helps tremendously in scores like the way Strauss writes, he writes that, he wants that C a lot of times. And of course, the modern composers like Prokofius, the Cicloish and all those guys, they have written, they want that, those low notes.
Well, back specifically to the right hand, what are the different ways of playing bass that you've seen them do with the right hand? Making...
You mean the bow or the...
Well, without the bow.

Well, everybody has his own style of how to hold their fingers, you know. A lot of guys just use one finger, a lot of guys use two. Of course, the best way is to put your thumb on the fingerboard, and you get a good leverage that way. And you use two fingers, the index and what you call this finger after... That's what you call it. It has had that famous finger, and you use those two, you alternate them. And that way, you can get a tremendous amount of agility and speed. And again, like I've seen some guys just use one finger... Oh, that's a mess. In other words, let's put it this way. A bass playing is an art. Practice, you know, like, it's the only way you can achieve anything is by practicing, especially an instrument. So, like, I mean, all these fakers running around. Sooner or later, they get discovered, and they're nowhere. It's best to work from the top up. And I'm glad things happened to me the way they did, because I started playing. I studied very seriously, and I was a long hair for a long time, and gradually this jazz bit came into my view, and it didn't jump on me all of a

sudden. And I'm glad it happened that way. Well, now, uh, what other way do they use other than holding their thumb against the finger bone and ticking with the first two fingers? What else have you seen
throughout the years? Oh, I really hadn't paid much attention. I'm thinking about the old slap bass.
Oh, I've seen slap bass, yeah. What is slap bass exactly? I don't know. I've never been able to do it

myself, to tell you the truth. It's just that you bounce the string up and down the fingerboard while you're playing. You hit the fingerboard with the string. Yeah, and while you're playing the notes with your left hand, you get a certain percussive effect that way. But it's gone out of style, sort of. I think a nice booming pizzicato bass is much nicer. I was to show you that jazz is going right in there, into the real nice musical all the way feeling, you know?
What about bowling now? Do the jazz musicians bow like the legit men?

Well, they have to now, you know. Practically every bass player is expected to bow a chorus, and that's where a good bass player is, can be picked out. I mean, well, you gotta know how to hold your bow, and you gotta know how to phrase your notes with the left hand and the coordination of the two hands. And I'm glad, I'm glad, I'm so glad to see that because years ago I used to try in bow courses and guys used to just laugh at me, you know? I'm so glad to see that now that practically, well, I won't say practically all of it, but a lot of tunes, now they give a bass player a bowing lick, you know, which is real nice. When was it that you bowed? Oh, it was quite a few years ago. I tried in different bands and I got kind of scorned that so I didn't try it anymore, you know?
was very popular with it in the...
Yeah, but he hummed along.
Yeah.
You know?
And you weren't trying to...

And in those days, I think that they were just saying, well, man, who do you think you are imitating Slam Stewart? Like, so these guys today, they're imitating Slam Stewart? No, they don't sound at all like Slam Stewart. They have their own individual way of playing. So I'm glad to see that. I think it's real nice. I could hear two choruses of it. Don't worry about that.
Okay.
I'll take care of it.
Now, which style of bowing do the jazz musicians generally use French or German?

Oh, either way, you can... There is a... I would say it's a 50-50 proposition in this country. It's about 50% play French bow, 50% play German bow. And I tell you, if I were a conductor in the symphony orchestra, I would try to have a French bow and a German bow divided into each stand, because each bow has a very good advantage. Now, with the French bow, you can play saltellato and spiccato real well. And with the German bow, you can play a good, loud attack, real good, strong notes, you know. So blending the two in a bass section of eight bass players, I think you get a real fine bass section. So I have nothing to say bad against neither the French bow nor the German bow. I think they both have an equal amount of advantage if you put them together.
What do you do, a bow like this and grab it on the end? So that way you've arrived at a compromise? No, I mean, which do you use?
I've been using the German bow. I've been using the German bow.
See? And how long has it been since you've played?
Oh, it's been about, I think it's been about three years since I last played.
And where was that?
In the symphony here.
And you haven't even sat in or?
Oh, I've jammed a few times. Yeah, I've jammed. A few blues and stuff like that. But in other words, I plan to pick it up when I go up to Italy.
You're going to Italy?

Yeah. I'm leaving as soon as my boat comes in. Oh, well, yeah. Now, I expect to do a lot of playing in Italy. In fact, more than I've been doing over here. Because there is a lot more going on over there than there is over here, as far as the arts are concerned.
Okay, we had it all for a second there. Go ahead, Rudy, about going to Italy.

Well, what I wanted to say, or I think would interest you, is that naturally I've been buying a lot of Italian magazines. I've been keeping up with the news in Italy. And I know there is a tremendous trend toward Dixieland music in Italy. They like it. They really love it. In fact, they have a lot of groups coming up. They may not sound like the original Dixieland that we have in America, but at least they're trying. And, boy, I give them credit. Because they like it and they're trying very hard to do it. And I expect I'm going to be doing a lot of playing, and I might even be able to help some of these groups along with what little I learned here in New Orleans. But, well, you know, when Louis Armstrong went to Italy, he got sick in Italy, you know. I got letters back from Italy telling me how glad they were that he was there and that, you know, and how I enjoyed his playing and how... And they asked me very important questions. And I even read an article where somebody was against jazz and they were having some kind of an argument about... Somebody called Shelley Mann a saxophone player.
Shelley Mann's a drummer, man.

Well, there you go. So there was a repercussion letter in the bottom saying, how can you talk about jazz against jazz if you don't even know what you're talking about, which was a very good point. So you see, from those arguments, you can see that they like jazz over there and they want it and they're getting it. They want to improve on it and they're going to improve on it. I think it's a wonderful thing.
Do you think any Italian music has gone into jazz? Do you hear any of it?

I don't know. I've heard hardly anything that would give you any sign of that. But of course, what you hear here is limited. Once I get over there, I might be able to form an opinion to that effect. But right now, I don't know.
Oh, Wingy swings out on us all on me. Oh, Wingy Manon.
Yeah.
Let's see. And the sax set from Lucia goes into... Kiodori did that. And blues for Jimmy on the Columbia record.
He had a Mordecai or Bodat on the bass, you know.

Those guys listen to opera. Bechet used to go down. Oh, yeah. The jazz musicians here. Obviously, they listen to opera. Oh, of course. And of course, we had that French opera here, which presented all kind of opera. You know, many of the famous Italian operas had their premiere at the French opera.
Oh, right. For this country. For this country.
That's something that people really aren't aware of.

No. Especially people in New York. Tell them something like that. They say, what? It's true. A lot of American premieres of operas have taken place right here in New Orleans at the old French opera house. By the way, do you think they'll ever rebuild a new French opera house? I've heard rumors the other day that they might.
Not in the same location?
No. Of course not.
With Permanentoulo, something's going to happen. Are they going to build a hotel?
Mm-hmm.
I believe. I don't think that just about winds it up unless you've got something else to say.
Well, that's about it. I can't think of anything else right now in Dick Allen. And it certainly has been a pleasure.
I thought of something.
What?

Since it's been a pleasure. What do you think is going to happen to the New Orleans style jazz in terms of the brass band guys, you know, and the people like that you saw who really were creative and did something really special that's uniquely New Orleans? Do you think that's going to live, be carried on?
Oh, I'm definitely positively sure that it'll be carried on. Of course it will. No question about it. It's ridiculous to even...
You think it'll be carried on here in the city?
Yes. It'll definitely be carried on here in the city and I have reasons to believe that it'll be carried on elsewhere. Like I got through saying a while ago, they're trying to do it in Italy.
You know, we see some pretty young guys out there in the street with the young tuxedo every once in a while. You'll see a guy in his 40s.
Yeah. Oh, yeah.
And then sometimes 30s and I've even seen a teenager or two out there.
Oh, yeah.
They may not have been great, but they wouldn't have been great.

No. Sooner or later, they all get over to it. You've got to. You're bound to it. It's a sort of a magnet. Of course, right now with this rock and roll and all this business, naturally, all the young kids aren't paying much attention to it. But as soon as that passes over, like Sir Thomas Beecham says, it will. You'll see that it'll just keep on going along its road like it always has been. And I think this is just a period where it's just sort of, let's say, hibernating. Not hibernating by itself, but through the fact that these other mediums have temporarily come up. And that, my dear boy, is the way I feel about it. Yeah. Did we leave anything out?
Probably so.
How long have we been here?
Well, we've got about, almost an hour and I have a tape and I think that's enough.
Oh, yeah.
That's plenty, Rudy. And thanks again.
You're welcome.
Au revoir. But not yet, that. stuff like stuff
